web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: Chapter 7: What the Price Assumes — Reverse DCF & Peer Multiples
question: What growth rate and cash-flow durability does ANET's $197.29 share price already embed, and how does that compare with networking and AI compute peers?

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get.
epigraph.author: Warren Buffett

web_blocks.title: 7.1 Deconstructing $197.29: Current Multiples vs. Five-Year History

web_blocks.html: At the November 13, 2026 close of $197.29, Arista Networks holds a $249.26 billion market cap [22]. Subtracting $14.36 billion in cash and securities—with zero funded debt—leaves an enterprise value of $234.90 billion [2][22]. Trailing twelve-month results show $11.89 billion in revenue, $4.75 billion in net income, and ~$5.02 billion in free cash flow [22]. Against those figures, the stock trades at 52.97x trailing P/E, 44.28x EV/EBITDA, 19.76x EV/Sales, and 49.68x P/FCF [22]. Looking ahead, consensus FY2027 Non-GAAP EPS of $6.02–$6.04 implies a 32.60x Forward P/E and a 0.91 PEG ratio [22][24].

Those multiples sit 22% to 44% above Arista's five-year averages of ~40.5x–43.5x trailing P/E and 13.7x EV/Sales [25]. Two structural shifts explain why the market pays this premium. First, revenue growth has sped up rather than slowed with scale. TTM sales are up 40.74% YoY, while Q3 2026 jumped 58.5% YoY to $3.66 billion—the fastest pace since Arista's 2014 IPO [3][22]. Second, operating leverage lifted Q3 2026 operating margin to 44.9% GAAP (49.1% non-GAAP) alongside a 28.89% ROIC [3][22]. When a $12 billion business grows near 40%–50% with zero debt and 45%+ cash conversion, standard hardware multiples fall short.

web_blocks.takeaway: At $197.29, ANET is expensive on trailing multiples (52.97x P/E, 19.76x EV/Sales) relative to its 5-year history, but trades at 32.60x FY2027E EPS and 26.8x FY2028E EPS—a sub-1.0x PEG if management delivers on its $18.5B FY2027 trajectory.

web_blocks.title: 7.2 Reverse DCF: What $197.29 Already Prices In

web_blocks.html: Rather than guessing fair value from one forecast, a Reverse DCF asks what 10-year sales growth justifies today's $234.90 billion enterprise value. We start from $11.89 billion in TTM revenue and a steady 44.0% unlevered free cash flow margin. That margin sits slightly below FY2025's 47.2% to reflect heavier AI hardware mix. We apply a 9.5% weighted average cost of capital (5.10% 10-year Treasury plus 4.4% equity risk premium). Beyond Year 10, we assume 3.5% terminal growth. Under those inputs, today's price implies a 16.0% 10-year revenue CAGR, solving to $196.16 per share.

web_blocks.title: Reverse DCF Implied 10-Year Revenue CAGR & Intrinsic Value
web_blocks.the_number: $197.29 embeds a 16.0% 10-year revenue CAGR ($196.16/sh at 44% FCF margin and 9.5% WACC). An 18.8% CAGR yields $239.39/sh.
web_blocks.how_calculated: Discount 10 years of free cash flows (Revenue x 44% FCF margin) plus a Gordon Growth terminal value (Year 10 FCF x 1.035 / (WACC - 0.035)) at 9.5% WACC. Add $14.36B net cash and divide by 1.2634B diluted shares.
web_blocks.the_inputs: TTM revenue $11.89B [22]; FY2025 FCF margin 47.2% normalized to 44.0% [1]; net cash $14.36B [2]; 1.2634B shares ($249.26B / $197.29) [22]; 10Y Treasury 5.10% + 4.4% ERP = 9.5% WACC.
web_blocks.the_range: At 15.0% CAGR and 10.5% WACC, implied value falls to $154.54. At 18.8% CAGR and 9.5% WACC, value reaches $239.39. At 22.0% CAGR and 8.5% WACC, value climbs to $371.77.
web_blocks.if_off: If hyperscaler AI spending pauses in 2027–2028 and 10-year growth slows to 14.0% (at 9.5% WACC), fair value drops to $170.24 (-13.7%). That signals downside toward the $150–$172 support band.

web_blocks.caption: Reverse DCF Sensitivity Matrix: Implied Share Price Across WACC & 10-Year Revenue CAGR (44% FCF Margin, 3.5% Terminal Growth)
web_blocks.takeaway: Because Arista is already guiding +48% revenue growth in FY2026 ($13.3B+) and +38%–40% in FY2027 ($18.5B), the market's 16.0% 10-year implied CAGR leaves a reasonable margin of safety if growth merely decelerates gracefully to ~10%–12% in Years 3–10.

web_blocks.title: 7.3 Peer Comparison: Networking Incumbents vs. AI Silicon

web_blocks.html: Comparing Arista with networking incumbents (Cisco, HPE, Celestica) and AI chip leaders (NVIDIA, Broadcom) shows a sharp split between multiples and tape structure. Cisco trades at 25.49x TTM P/E, 16.09x Forward P/E, and 5.83x EV/Sales [22]. HPE trades at 25.18x TTM P/E, 10.22x Forward P/E, and 1.87x EV/Sales [22]. Both carry steep discounts because their operating margins (27.12% and 8.03%) and M&A-aided growth (16.05% and 26.63%) trail Arista's 43.83% margin and 40.74% organic growth [22]. Even more striking, NVIDIA (10.34x Forward P/E, 0.16 PEG) and Broadcom (17.96x Forward P/E, 0.28 PEG) trade far lower. They sell at half to one-third of Arista's forward multiple despite faster TTM sales growth. Yet both chipmakers sit in Stage 4 downtrends while Arista holds Stage 2 leadership.

web_blocks.caption: Peer Valuation, Profitability & Stage Comparison (As of 2026-11-13)
web_blocks.takeaway: ANET commands the highest forward P/E (32.60x) and EV/Sales (19.76x) in the group, justified by 43.83% operating margins and sole Stage 2 technical leadership while all five peers sit in Stage 4.

web_blocks.mechanism: During the 1998–2000 telecom/internet buildout, Cisco's revenue compounded >45% annually and its P/E expanded past 100x; when carrier capex froze in 2001, revenue dropped 30% sequentially and valuation compressed to ~20x.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Cisco peaked near $80/share (~$555B market cap, >100x P/E) in March 2000 before falling ~88% to $8.60 in October 2002 despite remaining profitable.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Even elite networking franchises suffer violent multiple compression when capex cycles pause; ANET at 32.6x forward P/E is far saner than 100x in 2000, but $11.4B in purchase commitments means any hyperscaler digestion could compress P/E toward 22x–25x.

book_paragraphs: Now that we know what Arista builds and how cleanly it turns revenue into cash, we have to answer the hardest question in investing: is a great business already too expensive at $197.29? On the surface, the price tag looks steep. At $197.29 per share, the market values Arista at $249.26 billion. Even after subtracting $14.36 billion in net cash, you are paying $234.90 billion for the operating business—nearly twenty times trailing sales and fifty times trailing free cash flow.

Compared with Arista's own five-year history, those multiples sit 22% to 44% above average. Over the past half-decade, the stock typically traded around 40x to 43x trailing earnings and 13.7x enterprise value to sales. Today's premium exists for a simple reason: growth has accelerated rather than slowed. In Q3 2026, revenue surged 58.5% year-over-year to $3.66 billion, while GAAP operating margins hit 44.9%. When you look ahead to consensus FY2027 earnings of $6.02 to $6.04 per share, the forward P/E drops to 32.6x, giving a PEG ratio of 0.91.

book_subsections.title: Running the Reverse DCF: What Growth Must Happen?
paragraphs: Instead of pretending we can predict 2036 earnings to the penny, let us flip the math around and ask what 10-year revenue growth rate today's price already assumes. Start with $11.89 billion in trailing revenue, assume Arista converts 44% of future sales into free cash flow, and discount those cash flows at 9.5% with 3.5% terminal growth thereafter. At those settings, $197.29 per share breaks even at a 16.0% compound annual revenue growth rate over the next decade.

Think about what that means for you as an owner. Management is guiding for roughly 48% revenue growth in FY2026 and 38% to 40% growth in FY2027 toward $18.5 billion. To justify $197.29, Arista does not need to grow 40% forever. If it hits $18.5 billion in FY2027 and then slows all the way down to 10% or 11% annual growth from 2028 through 2036, it still clears the 16.0% 10-year hurdle. If instead Arista compounds at 18.8% annually over ten years, intrinsic value rises to roughly $239 per share—close to Wall Street's $236 to $250 post-Q3 targets.

book_subsections.title: Why ANET Costs More Than Cisco, HPE, and Even NVIDIA
paragraphs: Look across the peer table and a puzzle jumps out. Cisco trades at 16.1x forward earnings. HPE trades at 10.2x. Even NVIDIA—the undisputed king of AI compute—trades at 10.3x forward earnings, while Broadcom trades at 18.0x. Why does Arista command 32.6x forward earnings when AI chipmakers trade at half that multiple?

Part of the answer is business quality: Arista's 43.8% operating margin towers over Cisco's 27.1% and HPE's 8.0%, with zero debt and software-like EOS stickiness. Another part is institutional positioning: every single peer in that comparison—Cisco, HPE, Celestica, NVIDIA, and Broadcom—is currently locked in a Stage 4 downtrend. Arista is the sole Stage 2 leader standing above its moving averages, which concentrates institutional capital into the one chart that has not broken. Still, that multiple gap is a double-edged sword: if AI capex slows, a 32.6x forward multiple has further to fall than 10.3x. Next, we examine the price chart itself to see whether institutional buying is holding the floor.

book_subsections.title: Stress-Testing the Margin of Safety Across Interest Rates
paragraphs: A Reverse DCF is only as honest as its discount rate and margin assumptions. With the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield sitting at 5.10%, we use a 9.5% weighted average cost of capital—roughly four and a half percentage points above risk-free government bonds—and normalize Arista's free cash flow margin from 47.2% down to 44.0% to reflect heavier AI hardware mix. Even under those conservative settings, $197.29 per share only requires 16.0% compound annual revenue growth over the next ten years.

Now test what happens if rates move or growth stumbles. If the discount rate rises to 10.5% while 10-year revenue growth slows to 15.0%, intrinsic value drops to $154.54—roughly 22% below today's price. Conversely, if Arista compounds revenue at 18.8% annually at a 9.5% discount rate, intrinsic value rises to $239.39. If AI networking scales into a 22.0% decade-long compounder and long-term rates ease toward 8.5%, the math stretches past $370. That spread tells you why execution over the next six quarters matters so much: the stock is not priced for perfection, yet it leaves zero room for a multi-year stall.

callouts.title: The Cisco 2000 Lesson: Multiple Compression Hurts More Than Earnings Misses
callouts.text: In March 2000, Cisco Systems traded above 100 times earnings when carrier capital spending seemed unstoppable. When telecom orders froze in 2001, Cisco remained profitable, yet its stock fell 88% because the multiple collapsed to 20 times. Arista at 32.6 times forward earnings is nowhere near 2000-era bubble territory, but if hyperscalers digest capacity in 2027, a compression from 32.6x down to 25x forward earnings would pull the stock toward $150 even without an operating loss.

book_subsections.title: Wall Street Targets and What Consensus Still Misses
paragraphs: Following the November 3, 2026 Q3 earnings beat, Wall Street analysts raised their numbers across the board. Citigroup reiterated a Buy rating and lifted its price target from $215 to $248, Barclays maintained Overweight at $236, and the broader Street consensus target sits near $250.36. Consensus models now look for $13.38 billion to $13.39 billion in FY2026 revenue, $18.50 billion to $18.75 billion in FY2027 revenue with $6.02 to $6.04 in non-GAAP EPS, and $7.35 in FY2028 EPS.

Notice what consensus is still debating. Skeptics point to NVIDIA's Spectrum-X Ethernet bundle and question whether Arista can defend 64% gross margins as 800-Gigabit and 1.6-Terabit AI back-end clusters scale. Bulls point to $6.84 billion in deferred revenue and $11.4 billion in purchase commitments as hard proof that hyperscalers are locking in Arista's Etherlink roadmap through 2027 and 2028.

book_subsections.title: Why a Sub-1.0x PEG Ratio Changes the Valuation Debate
paragraphs: Investors who stop at the 52.97x trailing P/E ratio miss half the picture. Trailing earnings still reflect late-2025 and early-2026 shipments before Q3 2026's 58.5% surge took full effect. Looking forward to consensus FY2027 non-GAAP EPS of $6.02 to $6.04, the multiple compresses to 32.60x, and dividing that forward multiple by consensus five-year earnings growth of 35.94% yields a PEG ratio of 0.91.

That does not make the stock risk-free—a 19.76x EV/Sales multiple still demands high margins and durable demand—but it explains why institutional buyers have stepped in around $183 to $196 whenever macro volatility shakes the broader market.

book_subsections.title: Comparing Valuation Multiples Against Quality-Adjusted Peers
paragraphs: When you place Arista beside Cisco, HPE, Celestica, NVIDIA, and Broadcom, remember that raw P/E ratios never tell the whole story without margins and capital intensity. HPE trades at 10.2x forward earnings because its operating margin is 8.0% and its balance sheet carries acquisition debt. Celestica trades at 10.8x forward earnings because contract manufacturing earns an 8.6% operating margin. Arista earns 43.8% trailing operating margins with zero debt and 28.9% ROIC—justifying a structural premium over hardware assemblers and legacy incumbents, even while requiring disciplined entry pricing.

book_subsections.title: What Would Make Today's Valuation Expensive Overnight
paragraphs: Fair value is never static; it moves with growth durability. At $197.29, Arista's 16.0% implied 10-year revenue CAGR looks very achievable against a 38% to 48% near-term run rate. That changes quickly if AI cluster spending pauses in 2027 and multi-year revenue growth drops toward 12%—in which case a 9.5% discount rate pulls intrinsic value down toward $155 to $170, leaving little cushion for late buyers.

book_subsections.title: Why Free Cash Flow Conversion Justifies a Higher Floor
paragraphs: Traditional hardware makers often trade at 12x to 15x earnings because they must reinvest most of their profits into factories, inventory, and debt service. Arista converts 47.2% of revenue into free cash flow while spending barely 1.1% on capital expenditures. When a business generates that much distributable cash per dollar of sales, every point of revenue growth creates far more intrinsic value than an equivalent point of growth at a capital-intensive peer like HPE or Celestica—which is why our Reverse DCF anchors on 44% normalized free cash flow margins rather than hardware-sector norms.
